h2: Fired heater and furnace tubes: why they need a different inspection plan
html:
Fired heater and furnace tubes: why they need a different inspection plan

Short answer: exchanger tubes are examined from the bore with eddy current or IRIS. Fired heater tubes are steel coils inside a firebox, where the threats are creep, overheating and metal loss on both the fire side and the process side. Their plan therefore rests on visual examination, thickness and diameter measurement, on-stream thermography and, where the coil can be pigged, in-line ultrasonic tools.

What changes when the tube sits in a firebox

  • Temperature drives the damage. Radiant tubes run hot enough for creep, so a tube can swell and fail with plenty of wall left. Thickness alone does not tell you its condition.
  • Two sides corrode. Sulfidation or naphthenic acid can thin the bore in crude and vacuum service while oxidation and scaling work on the outside.
  • The governing documents differ. Heaters are inspected under API RP 573, and tube retirement thickness traces back to the design basis in API Standard 530, not to the exchanger references above.
  • The convection section hides its tubes. Finned and studded rows behind the shock tubes are hard to reach, and flue-gas dew point corrosion attacks the coolest rows.

Methods that answer heater-tube questions

On stream, infrared thermography through the sight doors maps tube metal temperature and finds flame impingement and hot spots, provided emissivity and reflected flame are corrected for. During the shutdown, a visual examination of the radiant box looks for bulging, sagging, bowing and scale; ultrasonic thickness readings on prepared spots give remaining wall; and diameter measurements against the baseline show creep swell. Hardness and alloy verification add evidence on metallurgical condition. Serpentine coils with pigging access can be scanned end to end by specialist in-line ultrasonic tools, which map wall thickness and deformation along the whole coil.

The remaining-life judgement belongs to the owner's engineer; the inspection's job is to give that engineer temperature history, wall and diameter data they can trust. Our full guide covers the damage mechanisms, the method choice and a turnaround scope checklist: fired heater tube inspection methods under API 573.
